title: Antonio Gramsci

cards.b:
Antonio Gramsci (1891–1937) was a founder of the Italian Communist Party. In 1926, Mussolini's fascist regime jailed him. At his trial, the prosecutor reportedly said: "we must stop this brain from working for twenty years."

It did not work. In prison he filled 33 notebooks, published after his death as the Prison Notebooks.

He asked a question Marx could not answer: why did workers in the West not revolt? His answer, hegemony, is now used across politics, media and cultural studies.

Ruling classes rule in two ways: by force (coercion) and by consent.

Hegemony is rule by consent. The ruling class makes its own interests look like common sense, natural and good for everyone. People accept their position not because they are forced, but because they come to believe in it.

So the bourgeoisie rules not only through the police and the army, but through schools, churches, newspapers and popular culture.

Gramsci's formula: the integral state = political society + civil society. Put another way, the state is hegemony protected by the armour of coercion.

Note the twist. For Marx, civil society meant the economy. For Gramsci, it is part of the superstructure: the world of ideas and institutions.

cards.h: War of position, war of manoeuvre
cards.b:
War of manoeuvre

A direct frontal attack on the state, as in the Russian Revolution of 1917. It worked in Russia because the state was everything and civil society was weak.

War of position

In the West, civil society is a strong system of "trenches". So revolution needs a long struggle to win hearts and minds first: building counter-hegemony in culture, schools and unions.

This shifted Marxism from economics toward culture and ideas.

"All men are intellectuals," Gramsci said, but not all have the function of intellectuals in society.

  • Traditional intellectuals, such as priests and academics, see themselves as independent of class.
  • Organic intellectuals grow out of a class and give it awareness of its role. The working class needs its own.

A historic bloc is an alliance of classes held together by a shared worldview. Gramsci wanted a bloc of northern workers and southern peasants in Italy.

He called the party the Modern Prince, after Machiavelli.

Passive revolution is change from above. Elites bring in reforms to absorb pressure from below, without real power passing to the masses. Gramsci used it for Italy's unification (the Risorgimento).

On crisis, he wrote: "The old is dying and the new cannot be born; in this interregnum a great variety of morbid symptoms appear."

That line is quoted often today to describe populism and the crisis of liberal democracy.

• Hegemony is hard to measure. How do we know when consent is real or manufactured?
  • The notebooks are fragments written in code to avoid prison censors. Readers disagree on what he meant.
  • Perry Anderson's essay "The Antinomies of Antonio Gramsci" (1976) showed that Gramsci uses "state" and "civil society" in shifting ways.
  • Ernesto Laclau and Chantal Mouffe moved hegemony beyond class altogether, in Hegemony and Socialist Strategy (1985).

Gramsci's idea of the "subaltern" classes inspired the Subaltern Studies group, started by Ranajit Guha in 1982. They rewrote Indian history from below.

Guha's Dominance without Hegemony (1997) argued the colonial state ruled India by coercion without winning real consent.

Partha Chatterjee and Sudipta Kaviraj read Indian independence as a passive revolution: Indian elites took power without fully transforming society.

quiz.q: Gramsci's hegemony means rule mainly through…
quiz.w: Hegemony is rule by consent, backed by coercion.

quiz.q: For Gramsci, civil society is part of…
quiz.w: Unlike Marx, Gramsci places civil society in the superstructure.

o: A long cultural struggle to win consent
quiz.w: It suits the West, where civil society is strong.
